lead: Blockchain features are real but conditional. Tamper-evidence, transparency, auditability, availability, pseudonymity, programmability and disintermediation each solve a problem, and each brings a cost: collusion risk, lost privacy, lower throughput, fees, key loss or oracle trust. This chapter pairs every claimed benefit with its limit, maps the main application areas, and tests common myths. Use it to judge a claim the way an engineer judges a quote: what is promised, what is the price, and what would make the promise fail?
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.3 on decentralization and the ledger view in Chapter 1.2.

blocks.text: A feature is a property of the design, not a guarantee for every use. Read each line as a pair: what the blockchain gives, and what it asks in return.

items: Tamper-evidence: each block stores a short fingerprint (hash) of the previous block, so changing an old transaction changes all later hashes. Limit: if colluding validators control more than 50% of power, they can rewrite recent history. Evidence is not proof against a majority.
Transparency: every participant can read the ledger and verify rules. Limit: salaries, prices and customer names become visible; privacy needs encryption, private channels or zero-knowledge proofs.
Auditability: the append-only history lets an auditor replay every entry. Limit: a false entry is audited as faithfully as a true one; auditability does not clean the input.

Availability and throughput: many replicas keep the ledger online through node failures. Limit: every node repeats validation, so public chains often process few transactions per second and peak demand raises fees.
Pseudonymity: a user acts through keys and addresses, not a name. Limit: addresses are public and linkable; one KYC exchange or delivery address can expose the full history. See Unit 2, cryptography.
Programmability: smart contracts run business rules on-chain. Limit: a bug is public and may be irreversible, and code is not automatically law. See Unit 5, Ethereum and smart contracts.
Disintermediation: a shared ledger can replace a reconciling middleman. Limit: outside facts still enter through an oracle, and governance of the ledger remains a human problem.

sections.h3: Potential: a map, not a promise

blocks.text: Potential means where the feature fits, not where it is already proved. Use this map to place an application, then ask who writes, who validates and who pays. See Unit 6 for details.

items: Payments: cross-border remittance and merchant settlement can shorten reconciliation between banks. A Chennai exporter still needs regulated on-ramps and off-ramps; the ledger settles the record, not the rupees in a bank account.
Records: land titles, degrees and insurance claims can share one append-only register. The registrar must still verify the first entry; a blockchain cannot decide who owns a plot.
Supply chains: drug, coffee or auto-parts batches can carry a shared trail from factory to shop. Sensors and warehouse staff feed the trail, so bad data remains bad.
Identity: a person can hold verifiable credentials and disclose only what is needed. Key loss and recovery become the hard part; a lost private key is not a lost password.
Voting: a voting ledger can give a public audit trail and one-vote tokens. It must also protect ballot secrecy and resist coercion at home; a public chain alone does neither.

blocks.text: A myth takes a conditional property and drops the condition. Test each claim with three questions: who can break it, what does the user reveal, and what does it cost?

items: Unhackable. Breaking SHA-256 is not the usual attack; capturing consensus is. A pool with 45% is below the line, but pools with 45% and 25% together hold 70%. A rewrite becomes possible when colluding hash power is above 50%; no chain is unhackable, only expensive to attack.
Anonymous. Public addresses are pseudonyms. Chain analysis groups addresses; an exchange record can attach a name.

Always cheaper or faster. Public chains charge per transaction and repeat work on many nodes. A ₹40 fee on a small payment is expensive; a permissioned chain may be faster but trusts fewer validators. Compare fees, energy, throughput and integration.
Trustless. No third party is not zero trust. Trust moves to miners or validators, wallet software, stablecoin issuers and oracles. The better word is trust-minimized.

On-chain data and code are always true or legal. The chain proves data was written and not changed, not that it matches reality. A forged invoice remains forged on-chain, and a court decides whether a contract is valid.

blocks.where: s₁ to sₖ are the hash-power shares of the colluding pools; k is their count. A rewrite risk exists when the colluding share is greater than 50%.

figure.caption: A single 45% pool stays below 50%, but the top two pools total 70% and break unhackability; public addresses break anonymity; 100 transactions at ₹40 cost ₹4,000 and break the free claim. All three fail, while tamper-evidence and availability remain real.

spec.title: Testing three claims
spec.aria: A flowchart tests a startup's three claims on a public chain: one 45% pool stays below 50% but the top two pools total 70% and break unhackability, public addresses break anonymity, and 100 transactions at ₹40 cost ₹4,000 and break the free claim, so all three fail though tamper-evidence and availability remain real.

examples.question: A startup claims its public blockchain is unhackable, anonymous and free. It has five mining pools with hash shares 45%, 25%, 15%, 10% and 5%. All transaction addresses are public. The average fee is ₹40 per transaction. Test each claim and state which fail.
steps: Unhackable, single pool: the largest share is 45%. Since 45% < 50%, one pool alone cannot control consensus.
Unhackable, collusion: sort the shares as 45%, 25%, 15%, 10%, 5%. The top two pools hold 45 + 25 = 70%. Since 70% > 50%, two pools can collude to exceed a majority; the absolute claim fails.

Anonymous: all addresses are public, so every transfer is visible. If one address is linked to a name through KYC or delivery data, its history is exposed; the claim fails and the system is only pseudonymous.
Free: the fee is ₹40 per transaction. For 100 transactions the cost is 100 × ₹40 = ₹4,000, so the claim fails.
Result: all three claims fail as stated, even though the chain has real tamper-evidence and availability.
examples.answer: All three claims fail: the top two pools reach 70% collusion, addresses are public, and 100 transactions cost ₹4,000 at ₹40 each.
examples.check:
shares = [45, 25, 15, 10, 5]
top = max(shares)
top_two = sum(sorted(shares, reverse=True)[:2])
fee = 40
cost_100 = 100 * fee
print(top)
print(top_two)
print(fee)
print(cost_100)

traps: Tamper-evident is not tamper-proof; 51% collusion can rewrite recent history, not the entire chain.
Pseudonymous is not anonymous; public addresses are linkable and can be tied to names by exchanges.
Trustless is shorthand for trust-minimized; oracles, wallets and validators still carry trust.
On-chain data is verifiable as written, not true; a forged invoice stays forged, and a court decides legality.
Always cheaper or faster is not a feature; compare fees, energy, throughput and integration.

quiz.q: List any four features of a blockchain.
quiz.a: Tamper-evidence, transparency, auditability, availability, pseudonymity, programmability or disintermediation.

quiz.q: Why can transparency be a business problem?
quiz.a: Competitors and customers can read prices, volumes or names; privacy then needs encryption or private channels.

quiz.q: Pools hold 45%, 25%, 15%, 10% and 5%. What is the two-pool colluding share? Does it cross 50%?
quiz.a: 45 + 25 = 70%; yes, 70% > 50%, so a two-pool majority is possible.

quiz.q: A forged land title is written on-chain. Does tamper-evidence make the title valid?
quiz.a: No. The chain proves the title was written and not later changed; the registrar must verify ownership before writing.
A user acts through keys or addresses, not a legal name; the address is public.
Trust is reduced, not removed: it moves to code, validators, oracles and wallet software.

quiz.q: A chain charges ₹40 per transaction. What do 250 transactions cost?
Why is a public voting ledger not automatically a good voting system?
quiz.a: It gives an audit trail, but ballot secrecy, coercion, voter eligibility and key recovery need separate design; a public chain alone can expose votes.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry work now moves from plain public chains to rollups, zero-knowledge proofs, oracle networks and verifiable credentials. Account abstraction tries to make key loss and recovery less brutal. Central banks are testing tokenised money and settlement ledgers. Search for “zero-knowledge proof”, “optimistic rollup”, “oracle problem” and “verifiable credential” to go further.
